title: Introduction to Treap
description: A randomized balanced search tree that is both a tree and a heap, and easy to code

sections.title: 12. Pitfalls and How to Think About It

blocks.text: A treap is a wonderfully clever data structure whose name is a blend of tree and heap. It is a binary search tree by key and a heap by a random priority, both at the same time.

That combination gives you a balanced search tree almost for free. Instead of the complex rotations of AVL or red black trees, a treap leans on randomness to stay balanced, which makes it far easier to understand and implement.

blocks.caption: Each treap node has a key and a random priority: a BST by key, a heap by priority
blocks.text: /engineering/dsa-media/1785406655549-62798518.png

By the end of this topic you will understand why plain search trees can go wrong, how mixing in random priorities fixes them, how the split and merge operations make a treap so flexible, and where treaps are used. It is one of the most elegant ideas in data structures.
The elegance is that you do not enforce balance directly at all. You attach a random number to each node and simply keep two ordinary rules true, and balance emerges on its own as a side effect.
A binary search tree gives fast lookups only when it is reasonably balanced. Its speed comes from halving the search space at each step, which needs a bushy, shallow shape.

blocks.caption: Inserting sorted data turns a plain BST into a slow straight line
blocks.text: /engineering/dsa-media/1785406655549-554174843.png

The trouble is that a plain BST does not control its own shape. If you insert keys in sorted order, each new key becomes the rightmost node, and the tree collapses into a straight line, effectively a linked list.

In that degenerate state, search, insertion, and deletion all slow to O(n), destroying the very advantage the tree was supposed to give. We need a way to keep the tree balanced no matter what order the keys arrive in.

items: A BST is fast only when it is balanced
A plain BST does not manage its own shape
Sorted input makes it degenerate into a line
In that state every operation slows to O(n)

blocks.text: Concretely, insert the keys 1 through 5 in order into a plain BST. Each key is larger than the last, so it hangs off the right of the previous one, and you end up with a five level chain instead of a bushy tree.

The core weakness:

A plain BST lets the input order dictate its shape. Balanced variants, including the treap, take control of the shape back from the input.
A treap solves this by giving every node two values: its key and a randomly chosen priority. The structure then obeys two rules at once.

blocks.caption: A treap is a BST on the keys and a max heap on the random priorities
blocks.text: /engineering/dsa-media/1785406655550-298351385.png

items: By key, it is a binary search tree: left subtree keys are smaller, right subtree keys are larger
By priority, it is a heap: every node has a higher priority than its children
Each node stores both a key and a random priority
Both properties hold simultaneously across the whole tree

blocks.text: The key ordering is what lets you search. The priority heap ordering is what forces the shape. The surprising fact is that these two rules together determine the tree almost uniquely, and with random priorities that shape is balanced.

Two rules, one tree:

Given a fixed set of keys and priorities, there is essentially only one valid treap. The keys decide the left to right order and the priorities decide the top to bottom order.

Trace the example tree: the keys 20, 30, 40, 50, 70 read in sorted order left to right, satisfying the BST rule, while the priorities decrease as you go down from the root, satisfying the heap rule. Both hold together.
Here is the beautiful part. Because priorities are random, the node that becomes the root is a random one, since the highest priority is equally likely to be any key.
A random root splits the keys into two roughly equal halves, just like picking a random pivot in quicksort. This happens recursively at every level, so the tree stays balanced on average.

The randomness is the whole trick. An adversary choosing a bad insertion order cannot hurt you, because the shape depends on the random priorities, not on the order the keys arrived. The expected height is about the logarithm of n.

The quicksort connection:

A treap built from random priorities has the same structure as a quicksort using random pivots. That is exactly why its expected height is logarithmic.
Because the highest priority key becomes the root, and that key is uniformly random, the root is essentially a random pivot. A random pivot tends to split the keys into two fairly even halves.

items: The maximum priority is equally likely to be any key
So the root is a random key, like a random pivot
A random pivot splits keys into roughly equal halves
This recurses, giving an expected height near log n

blocks.text: When an operation breaks the heap rule, a treap fixes it with a rotation, the same local restructuring used by other balanced trees.

blocks.caption: A rotation lifts a high priority child above its parent while keeping key order
blocks.text: /engineering/dsa-media/1785406655550-834017405.png

A rotation swaps a parent and a child while carefully preserving the left to right key order. The crucial property is that a rotation never breaks the BST ordering; it only changes which node sits higher.

So whenever a child ends up with a higher priority than its parent, a single rotation lifts the child above the parent, repairing the heap rule without disturbing the search order. Rotations are the low level move that all treap operations are built from.

items: A rotation swaps a parent and a child locally
It always preserves the BST key ordering
It is used to restore the heap priority ordering
Every treap operation is built from rotations, or from split and merge

blocks.text: The safety of rotations rests on one fact: a rotation only reorders the vertical relationship between a parent and child, never the horizontal key order. That is why it can fix the heap rule without ever breaking the search rule.

items: A rotation swaps a parent with one of its children
Left to right key order is always preserved
It is used to restore the heap priority order
Insertion rotates up, deletion rotates down

blocks.text: Inserting into a treap starts exactly like a plain BST. You descend by key and place the new node as a leaf in its correct position, then give it a random priority.

blocks.caption: Insert as a BST leaf, then rotate it upward while it beats its parent priority
blocks.text: /engineering/dsa-media/1785406655550-283659317.png

At that point the BST rule holds, but the heap rule might not, because the new leaf could have a higher priority than its parent. So you rotate it upward, one step at a time, as long as its priority beats its parent.
When its priority is finally smaller than its parent, the heap rule holds again and you stop. The new node bubbles up to exactly the level its random priority earns it, which keeps the tree balanced.

items: Descend by key and insert as a normal BST leaf
Assign the new node a random priority
Rotate it up while its priority exceeds its parent
Stop when the heap order is restored

blocks.text: Picture inserting a key that draws a very high random priority. It enters as a leaf, then rotates upward again and again until it reaches near the root, which is exactly where such a high priority node belongs.
Deletion is the mirror of insertion. To remove a node, you cannot just cut it out if it has two children, so instead you push it down until it becomes a leaf.

blocks.caption: To delete, rotate the node down toward its higher priority child until it is a leaf
blocks.text: /engineering/dsa-media/1785406655551-941190175.png
You repeatedly rotate the target downward, each time toward whichever child has the higher priority. This keeps the heap rule valid for the rest of the tree while the doomed node sinks.
Once the node reaches the bottom and becomes a leaf, it has no children to worry about, so you simply detach it. The tree remains a valid treap throughout.

items: A node with two children cannot be removed directly
Rotate it down toward its higher priority child
Repeat until the node becomes a leaf
Then detach the leaf, leaving a valid treap

blocks.text: Sinking the node rather than cutting it out is what keeps things simple. At every step you choose the higher priority child to rotate with, which preserves the heap rule for everyone except the node you are removing.

items: Locate the node to delete by its key
Rotate it down toward its higher priority child
Repeat until it is a leaf with no children
Detach the leaf, leaving a valid treap

blocks.text: Many modern treaps skip rotations entirely and build everything from two powerful operations: split and merge. This style is clean and very flexible.

blocks.caption: Split breaks a treap by key into two; merge joins two treaps into one
blocks.text: /engineering/dsa-media/1785406655551-600843207.png

Split takes a treap and a key, and breaks it into two valid treaps: one with all keys below the split key, and one with the rest. Merge does the reverse, joining two treaps into one, on the condition that every key in the first is smaller than every key in the second.

Notice how insertion becomes a one liner: split around the new key, then merge the pieces back together with the new node in between. Deletion is just as easy: split out the key and merge the remaining halves.

These two operations are the real superpower of a treap. Once you have split and merge, insertion, deletion, and even range operations all reduce to a couple of splits and merges, with no separate rotation code to maintain.

items: split(t, key): produces one treap with keys below the split and one with the rest
merge(a, b): joins two treaps when all of a keys are below all of b keys
insert: split around the key, then merge the new node between the halves
delete: split the key out, then merge the two remaining halves

blocks.text: The balance of a treap is a probabilistic guarantee, not a strict one. Because the priorities are random, the expected height of the tree is on the order of the logarithm of n.

It is possible, in principle, for random priorities to produce a tall tree, just as it is possible to flip many heads in a row. But the probability of a badly unbalanced treap is astronomically small, and no input order can force it.

Expected, not guaranteed:

A treap does not promise a logarithmic height every single time, but the chance of a bad shape is vanishingly small. In practice it behaves like a reliably balanced tree.

The intuition is the same as randomized quicksort. Just as random pivots make quicksort run in expected n log n, random priorities make a treap have expected logarithmic height, no matter how the keys arrive.
This is why a treap is called a randomized balanced BST: it does not fight to stay balanced, it simply borrows the reliability of randomness to make imbalance overwhelmingly unlikely.
With randomness keeping the height logarithmic, all the main operations are efficient in the expected sense.

items: Search: expected O(log n)
Insertion and deletion: expected O(log n)
Split and merge: expected O(log n)
Space: O(n), one node per key plus its priority

blocks.text: These bounds are expected values over the random priorities, and they hold regardless of the order in which keys are inserted, which is the key advantage over a plain BST.

Order does not matter:

Unlike a plain BST, a treap gives the same expected performance whether keys arrive sorted, reversed, or shuffled, because the shape follows the random priorities, not the input.
Treaps compete with AVL trees and red black trees, which also keep a search tree balanced. The difference is how they achieve it.

blocks.caption: Treaps trade the strict guarantees of AVL and red black trees for simplicity
blocks.text: /engineering/dsa-media/1785406655551-53139376.png

items: AVL and red black trees guarantee balance strictly, but their insertion and deletion logic is intricate
Treaps guarantee balance only in expectation, but are far simpler to implement correctly
Treaps offer clean split and merge operations that the others lack
For contests and many practical uses, the simplicity of a treap wins

blocks.text: If you need an ironclad worst case guarantee, a red black tree may be the choice. If you want a balanced tree you can write quickly and correctly, especially one supporting split and merge, a treap is hard to beat.

A practical point: the amount of code for a fully working treap with split and merge is a fraction of a correct red black tree. For interviews and contests, that difference in implementation risk is enormous.
Treaps show up wherever a flexible, balanced, ordered structure is needed without a lot of implementation pain.

items: Ordered sets and maps that also need to split and merge quickly
Competitive programming, where the simple code is a big advantage
The implicit treap variant, which indexes by position to support array like operations with fast range splits
Randomized data structures in general, where simplicity and good expected behaviour matter

blocks.text: The implicit treap is especially powerful: by using subtree sizes instead of keys, it can reverse or move whole ranges of a sequence in logarithmic time, something a plain array cannot do.

The implicit treap deserves special mention. By keying on subtree size instead of value, it represents a sequence and can insert, erase, reverse, or move an entire range in logarithmic time, powering advanced sequence problems.
In short, reach for a treap when you want ordered data with fast insert, delete, search, and especially fast split and merge, all with code you can trust to be correct.

content.title: 12. Pitfalls and How to Think About It

blocks.text: A few points keep a treap correct and keep your reasoning clear.

items: Use genuinely random priorities; predictable ones can be exploited to unbalance the tree
Remember both invariants at once: BST order by key, heap order by priority
Prefer split and merge for clean, flexible code over hand written rotations
The balance is expected, so think in terms of average behaviour, not a hard guarantee

blocks.text:
The mental model:

Sort left to right by key, stack top to bottom by random priority. The randomness of the priorities is what quietly keeps the whole tree balanced.
One more caution: seed your randomness well and use a wide range of priorities. If many nodes share the same priority, ties weaken the balance guarantee the randomness is supposed to provide.
The treap is proof that a little randomness can replace a lot of complicated bookkeeping.

items: A treap is a BST by key and a heap by a random priority at the same time
Random priorities keep the expected height logarithmic, whatever the input order
It balances with simple rotations, or with elegant split and merge operations
All operations run in expected O(log n)
It is far simpler than AVL or red black trees and supports fast split and merge

blocks.text: When you want a balanced ordered structure that is easy to get right, or you need to split and merge sequences fast, the treap is the tool to remember.
Carry this picture with you: keys sorted left to right, random priorities stacked highest at the top. Two simple rules, one random ingredient, and a tree that balances itself.
